utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Can we have the accused brought in, please? (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can now resume. Are our interpreters ready? Is everybody feeling good? We can resume. Does everybody hear? General Blaskic, do you hear, does the Defence hear, Prosecution, my colleagues? Ms. Paterson, I believe this is a protected witness that we are going to have brought in. I am listening to what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, as we explained at the end of the day yesterday, this witness has asked for full protection, she has asked to testify in a closed session and to be referred to by a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well then, the pseudonym will be what, what letter are you using?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we already used Witness A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe that the previous Witness A in fact really was Witness P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is a little strange. If A is P and R is S, I would like us to be specific here. Well, all right. I turn to Ms. Paterson. All right, so what is the letter then? What letter are we going to use, because we had rendered a decision about a Witness A.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is really up to the court. We would prefer to use Witness A for many reasons that would be easier for us, but if the court would prefer we call her Witness P, it does not honestly matter to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I am not mistaken, there have been prior discussions in the litigation about the protected nature of this witness, and she was referred to as Witness A during those discussions; for consistency it might be helpful to keep that appellation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right then, we will call her Witness A, but let me remind you, and my colleagues remember just as I do, that we had rendered a decision about Witness A which is not this Witness A, but so that we do not waste any time, we will call her Witness A but noting in the transcript that perhaps we should take another look at the other witness that we called Witness A. I am not going to give his name here, but everybody knows who I am talking about. All right, this is closed session, I believe the Defence agrees to that, completely closed. Very well, Mr. Hayman, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do, your Honour. For the record, we note this witness did give a media interview to Interpress News Agency in 1994, not using her name but describing her treatment. But we have no objection to the closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are right to remind us of that. The witnesses are protected by the Tribunal, but everyone must know that we can only ensure protection that we have jurisdiction over. We cannot protect witnesses who do not take minimal precautions for themselves. Thank you for telling us that. Ms. Paterson, this will now be a closed session, completely closed. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does everybody hear? Is everything technical working properly, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In principle it is working right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please excuse the judges for this slight delay, which is due to all of the motions that the parties have filed, so you see we are working for you in any case. Mr. Harmon, I believe, is going to take over the public Prosecutor's seat right now, as we say. Mr. Harmon, let me remind you that tomorrow we shall be completed at the very end of the morning, or the beginning of the afternoon. I would just like to recall this, and now you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours and counsel. Mr. President, the next witness we are going to call will be retired Major Erik Friis-Pedersen from the Danish army. His testimony will relate to counts 15 through 20 of the indictment. In summary, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If you do not mind, this is not something we are doing ritualistically, but I am asking for specifics here. I am not just going through a ritual we are going through in order to please Judge Jorda. I want this to relate to exactly what we are talking about, that is counts 15 to 20. This is inhumane treatment, taking of hostages and the use of human shields.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major Friis-Pedersen, Mr. President, served as an ECMM monitor in Central Bosnia from 26th January 1993 until the end of May 1993. His testimony will relate to five specific areas. First, he will identify a report that he prepared on 20th April 1993, describing the shells of the Hotel Vitez. This testimony, Mr. President, ties into the testimony of a previous witness who testified that on 20th April she and other civilians from the village of Gacice were taken to the Hotel Vitez and used as human shields. Secondly, Mr. President, he will describe his meetings with then Colonel Blaskic at the Kiseljak barracks prior to 16th April 1993, and his knowledge about civilian prisoners who were kept at the Kiseljak barracks after 16th April 1993. The third area he will testify about is he will describe the work of ICRC, the International Red Cross, in Central Bosnia and in particular what ICRC representatives told HVO commanders about the rights of prisoners and the obligations of commanders in relation to those prisoners. Fourthly, he will testify that he received information from a deputy commander of III Corps on 9th May that Darko Kraljevic was associated with the truck bomb that went off in Stari Vitez. Lastly, Mr. President and your Honours, he will testify about a threatening phone call which he received from Ante Valenta on the evening of 18th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for that summary. Let me quickly go through counts 15 to 20. Human shields is not something you are going to talk about here, since you did speak about 15 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, his testimony is essentially evidence that relates to the allegations that we have made in respect of human shields and is evidence that supports the testimony of the previous witness who testified about her experiences as a human shield around the Hotel Vitez on 20th April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, the witness could now be brought in. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would just like to say at some convenient time I would like to make a very short oral motion concerning the testimony of the last witness on the issue of hearsay. I can put it in writing if the court prefer, but I think in a minute or two I can state it orally. It really is a part of our previous submitted motion on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not think it needs to be in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Registrar, you will remind me of that. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Major Friis-Pedersen, first of all do you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please confirm to the Tribunal what your name and first name are before you take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first name is -- first names are Mogens Erik, family name is Friis-Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please read the declaration which will be given to you now. That will be your oath. MAJOR FRIIS-PEDERSEN (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. You may be seated. You were called by the Prosecutor as part of a trial being conducted against General Blaskic who is here, at the time he was Colonel Blaskic. Please testify about five points which were indicated very rapidly to us by the Prosecutor, having to do with the shelling of the Hotel Vitez, your meeting with General Blaskic, the description you will give us of the work you were doing, information about the truck bomb and possible responsibility of a person who is not here but who is related to the general context of this case and lastly the telephone call from Valenta. You will make your testimony first and then the Prosecutor may ask you some further questions. The judges and the Defence attorneys are also prepared to ask you questions. Mr. Harmon, proceed, please. Examined by MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Major Friis-Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to begin by describing your background and experience as a military officer to the judges of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was called in as a private in the Danish army, that was in 1955. In 1965, I got my commission as an officer, and working as such, various duties especially inside the communication corps, Second Corps in the Danish army, up until my retirement from the career, which took place in 1991. Since 1991, I have been listed in the reserve, you can do that in the Danish army, as a reserve officer until my age of 60, which will be in two years. During my military career before 1991, I was, among other things, on a few foreign courses away from Denmark. I served the last five years of my career, until 1991, in the NATO headquarters of NATO, NATO headquarters in Oslo called Afnorth. After I retired, I put myself at disposal from the Danish army, they could -- I volunteered for duties as UN observer or EC monitor, and that was the capacity I served as such from end of January 1993 until end of May the same year. Before in my career, I have to mention that I served as an UN military observer in the Middle East from 1978 to 1980. After my serving as an EC monitor, I should just mention that I also served as an UN military observer, same place in Yugoslavia, mainly in Kiseljak, two last months -- that was six months altogether, from November until end of April 1994. That was mainly in Kiseljak, which I know well, and then also in Macedonia. Because of my experiences as foreign service like UN and within EC, I was picked by the armed forces to serve in Finland as an instructor of the military observers course they have for Scandinavian officers there. That was in the beginning of 1995. From June 1995 until end of 1995, I was picked for UN military observer duty in Tajikistan. That is the end of what I can tell about my career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major. While you were an ECMM monitor in Central Bosnia, did you prepare daily operation reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did certainly, every day, it was at least as long as I was chairman, to preparing and responsible for sending them, but every day I participated in creating the operational reports that we should be sent from that team, or that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a daily operational report? Can you explain to the judges exactly what it is and where it is sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. A daily operational report from a team or a joint commission as we had Busovaca joint commission, is a summary of what the team or various teams attached to this unit have been doing during the day. It is composed of -- it is built up after a system that ECMM in Zagreb wanted us to build up after.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have Exhibit 187, which is the Prosecutor's next exhibit, if we can have that placed on the ELMO and distributed to judges and to counsel. Mr. President, for the record, Prosecutor's Exhibit 187 is in English, it is two pages, and two paragraphs from this particular daily operation report which Major Friis-Pedersen will be testifying about have been translated into French. Those are attached at the rear of the English daily operation report. Major, on the ELMO which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Could we have it, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was just reading this document, I just see that you do not have a copy of it. All right, that is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Major, on the ELMO to your right, there should appear in front of you on the monitor a daily operation report dated 20th April 1993. Did you prepare this particular daily operation report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did it in conjunction with my co-manager at that day, Henk Morsink, a Dutch ECMM monitor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to paragraph 3 on the first page. Can you please read that paragraph and explain that paragraph to the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 3 reads: "Cease-fire violations (unconfirmed). 2 T34 tanks were told to be in position on the mountain road between" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for a second. There was a significant difference, I do not think it is the interpreters, it is non-confirmed, is it, unconfirmed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Unconfirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, I think that the interpreters could not see the screen very well, so there is a slight error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not very good on my screen too, but I look here on my paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be moved up so the interpreters can see paragraph 3, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The text should be raised up on screen, then perhaps the light could be dimmed so that we get a better contrast. That is much better. Is that better for you too, Major? Do you see things better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, everybody is more comfortable that way, including the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes: "Cease-fire violations (unconfirmed). 2 T34 tanks were told to be in position on the mountain road between Zenica and Vitez. Shelling HVO HQ and the PTT building in Vitez. HVO is said to be putting an ultimatum on Gacice and after that failed, HVO is said to have started attacking this village."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, in that paragraph it says "HVO HQ". Does "HQ" stand for "headquarters"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information is unconfirmed. Can you explain to the court what unconfirmed information is and what the source of that information was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The source of the information was coming to us from BritBat operational room. We were situated in a place roughly 200 metres away from them, and we had regular, that means more than one daily contact between us, in those critical days here. Much sources of information who came to us came from BritBat, because they have armed means to go and look at spots more than we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find in your experience in the former Yugoslavia that the information that was provided to you by BritBat was reliable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were always reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn now to another subject, which is the Kiseljak barracks. Are you familiar with the Kiseljak barracks, Major Friis-Pedersen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I mentioned with my presentation concerning myself, I had been on station in Kiseljak for four months in late autumn and winter 1993-1994, and I lived exactly -- I rented a room in a private house there, situated roughly 200 or 300 metres away from the barracks, so I know exactly where the barracks and where, of course, the UN headquarters was in connection with Kiseljak there, it was a matter of less than one kilometre from the UN headquarters in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to 16th April 1993, did you have occasion to meet then Colonel Blaskic at the Kiseljak barracks? Could you explain to the judges the number of times and the circumstances under which you met him at that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, Colonel Blaskic I was introduced to the first time 22nd February. I am a little in doubt about the date, 21st or 23rd, but that day is what I believe it is. I met him in Kiseljak barracks, in a meeting room they had in there. As I understand, it was a local brigade in Kiseljak, local HVO brigade in Kiseljak, and Colonel Blaskic I met there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other occasions did you meet Colonel Blaskic at the Kiseljak barracks prior to 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it must have been one or two times more, I cannot recall any dates, but that was in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to ask Colonel Blaskic why he met you at both the Hotel Vitez and at the Kiseljak barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that during the first meeting in Vitez where I met him there, where I suppose that I should have a call back telling me, "please come to Kiseljak that and that day", I was a bit surprised he also appeared in Vitez, but it appeared to me later on that this is his real headquarters, the right headquarters, but as army commanders above a certain level always have at least two headquarters to work from. To me it is very natural that he told me, "I work both places" and that sometimes he is at one and sometimes at the other place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 16th April, Major Friis-Pedersen, were you aware that civilian prisoners were being detained at the Kiseljak army barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that and that was -- I think it was 18th April, I had to go to Kiseljak in some other business, also to talk to the HVO brigade there, and I had a hint from various sources before, that was BritBat and that was the commander of this checkpoint in Bilalovac, Klokati, who have hindered us in coming into Kiseljak the day before, who told me, "they have prisoners in there, among others my own wife and daughter". Some other men, some other women. I asked then the next day when I met this commander HVO also, the 18th, I think it was. I asked, "do you have prisoners here?". He confirmed to me, "yes, we have, around 120, up to 150, and among them two women and one child". As I knew, it was not the real way of exercising Geneva Conventions to have civilian child and women detained. I asked them, "could you give them now, those women and that child to me, because I want to take them back immediately". I could, and I got them with me, and delivered them back on their houses, which was in Kiseljak and Bilalovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO commander with whom you were talking point out the building in which the other prisoners were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had a meeting building where we always went to that was up the road in the barracks to the right, and to the left across some green areas, 50 to 100 metres away, were barracks where HVO men, the HVO commander pointed out to me, "okay, we have them over there". I asked if I could see them, because all information I could get about prisoners of war I would pass over to International Red Cross, they take action on those things, and also he pointed out to me where they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was about 50 to 100 metres away from the room where you normally met with Colonel Blaskic when you met with him in Kiseljak, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn to another subject, Major Friis-Pedersen, and that is the International Red Cross. Did you have occasion to work with the International Red Cross while you were an ECMM monitor in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially in the critical days around Easter and after Easter where these uprises or clashes went on, we had almost daily contact with the International Red Cross, a delegate from there especially, who were attached to this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court the practices that you observed and you were aware of the ICRC in respect of advising HVO commanders of their rights -- of prisoner rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I recall a meeting we had in our local monitor house close to BritBat, with the commander BritBat, this delegate of the Red Cross that was working with us, us white men. She told, that was the lady, she told what she is doing when she is approaching commanders -- International Red Cross, of course, directly go to the commander before they try to exercise any of their duties, which was that she would explain to the commanders the means of the Geneva Convention concerning prisoners of war, concerning treating of civilians during a conflict, and these rights were, of course, concerning prisoners of war, especially that they should be taken away as soon as -- taken prisoners away from the battle zone; they should be treated in a humanitarian way, they should get sufficient food, at least as good as their own troops, they should not be used as shields around military installations that enemy that took them; they should not be used as power for digging trenches or fortifications for that part. Concerning civilian prisoners, she told us she will explain them the rules again about how to treat them: you are not allowed to take civilians as prisoners and if you do for certain reasons, you have to free them again as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, with the help of the usher, please, I would like to take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 187 and if we could turn the page on 187 and have the part which is 8C shown on the monitor. This is also part of the daily operations report that you prepared on 20th April 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please read what you reported to in the daily operation report of that date under 8C, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, may I just clarify a little bit first?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first lines are, "the other monitor" so and so, and that means that we were two men there at that day taking care of duties in Vitez. Because we have several tasks to do and we had means of application and transportation, we divided into two. This is also my other monitor who gave this as his contribution to the daily situation report. He told me of the other monitor went together with the rest of the joint commission, that means the two officers we had for him and the representative of the International Red Cross, that was this delegate I talked about before, to HVO brigade headquarters in Vitez. We explained the condition of ICRC and the work of the joint commission. "The list were not ready", that means a list that the HVO has promised about which prisoners they held in Vitez: "The list was not ready, mainly because of communication problems. HVO agreed on providing list at the next day at 9.00, to be collected by ICRC and agreed", this HVO man, "agreed on the International Red Cross conditions about treating the visit and the rights of prisoners. The team stressed the security because of ten shooting incidents yesterday when the team was fired upon with small arms fire."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let me turn to another subject, Major. Did you have a conversation with Ramiz Dugalic, the deputy commander of III Corps, on 9th May 1993 about a truck bomb that exploded in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell the judges what you recall about that conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that he reported to me and my co-assistant, another monitor, that there were two men arrested by BiH in Ahmici some days before the 9th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the BiH or by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, by the HVO. No, it was BiH, excuse me, BiH went in at that time. BiH went in and captured those two men, they had the police signs of Croatia in their pockets. These men told us that we could interrogate them if we wanted. From this event further he told us, Mr. Dugalic, that the car bomb truck was actually driven by a Muslim humanitarian driver. He was not knowing what his cargo was, it proved to be this car bomb that made the big crater in the middle of Vitez, in the middle of the street. He was also arrested by HVO and forced to drive this car. There was another man behind the car that was named to us that he could give maybe evidence, that was Darko Kraljevic, he was living in Vitez in the, I think it was the part of Vitez very close to the road junction leading to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let me turn to the last subject and that is a threatening phone call that you received from a gentleman named Ante Valenta. Before you tell the judges about that phone call, let me ask the usher to place Exhibit 80/8 on the ELMO. While that exhibit is being brought and shown to you, Major Friis-Pedersen, do you know a gentleman by the name of Ante Valenta and had you had contact with him prior to this phone call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him. He was -- I can actually point him out. That is the man. I was told, I have no reason to doubt that, that he was the political advisor to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am finished with that photograph, Mr. Usher, thank you. Can you please describe to the judges of the Trial Chamber the telephone call that you received on the evening of 18th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was sitting in my office in the ECMM house in Vitez, close to BritBat, when the phone rang and I am not sure that Ante Valenta spoke sufficient English, so it was done with an interpreter in the ear of the phone, I listened to with my other ear so I could hear the voice of the man and she translated to me what he said. The thing was, it was a man unknown, he would not give his name or his phone number, or unit or anything, but what he said was that if BritBat did not stop helping the Muslim, as BritBat has done after the car bomb went off in Vitez, if they did not stop helping the Muslims and giving no help to the HVO side, they will attack BritBat. HVO will attack BritBat. That was the thing I got out of that conversation. As I could recognise by nearly -- well, between 90 and 100 per cent security, or what do you call it, I was nearly 90 to 100 per cent secure that this was a voice of Ante Valenta.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "secure", do you mean "certain"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Certainty", excuse me. Certainty 90 to 100 per cent that it was Ante Valenta. I had his phone number with me, I knew that he was attached to the headquarters of Colonel Blaskic in Vitez, and that matches very good with his phone number on the card. I phoned the number I had and got him on the telephone, and told him, "I have just a curious conversation coming in right before. It seemed to be your voice". He denied weakly, denied weakly. I never got a clear answer, "no, it was not me", but I did not get the opposite answer either. I explained to him what was said to us, and I explained back because I was a bit furious about this threatening phone call, because now the HVO claim to have the same right as the Muslims they have attacked by the car bomb, and the only one who helped the Muslims at that time, that was BritBat who put in all their forces just to secure the wounded refugees to come out to a special camp they installed a little outside Vitez. That was very well done. Now we have this threatening phone call, I explained Ante Valenta, this was indecent to come with such a threat, if that should really happen, BritBat to my experience -- excuse me. BritBat would only do one thing, and that was to withdraw the forces to the camp -- excuse me a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take your time, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seem to recover. BritBat would only do one thing to withdraw all the forces to camps, help nobody but defending themselves, and if they really launched a clash, they would suffer from this clash with the Brits, they had better arms, and at this spot they could resist. He received that report from me, okay, and no further talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Mr. President, I would now move to introduce into evidence Prosecutor's Exhibit 187. Thank you, Major Friis-Pedersen, I have concluded with my part of the examination. Now Defence counsel has an opportunity to question you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I congratulate for your conciseness and precision. I also thank the Major for his precision. Is it Mr. Hayman now? Very well, Mr. Hayman, on behalf of the Defence counsel, will have some questions for you within the framework of the cross-examination. Cross-examined by MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Major, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me call your attention first to paragraph 3 of Exhibit 187, do you have that with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it a daily report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the daily operational report dated 20th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 3 which is titled, "cease-fire violations (unconfirmed)". If a BritBat personnel member personally observed a violation of the cease-fire, would that be a confirmed or an unconfirmed violation as reported in your reports such as Exhibit 187?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be -- if he could confirm it, we rely totally on BritBat information. We had to do and it proved that it was solid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if BritBat saw it, you would list it under paragraph 2 "cease-fire violations (confirmed)", is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fact that the material listed under paragraph 3, unconfirmed cease-fire violations, does that mean that the information related therein was provided to BritBat by some other source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they have not been on the spot to confirm it themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told what that source was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to find out what the source was and the actual quality of the information, we would have to talk to someone other than yourself, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, yes. I have not yet been able to myself to confirm this thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember. We divided our means between us, we had normally mostly at that time two teams to go out with, only the one was armed, that was an armed Mercedes. The BritBats always went out with APCs, armed personnel cars. That gave a better way to get through if there should be troubles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not think, I take it, you were able to personally confirm the information in paragraph 3 on Exhibit 187, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but that is according to our procedure we have to divide with strictly confirmed that we know 100 per cent sure, that this happened, as in paragraph 2, you see, same message and the unconfirmed, we are not quite sure yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: BritBat received a report from some source that there was shelling, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that was a verbal report from BritBat Ops Room, as I told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any more specific information concerning when the report described in paragraph 3 stated or suggested that the shelling was? Was it at 3.00 in the morning, was it at noon, was it at 10.00 in the evening, was it one shell every minute all day long? Do you have any more information in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it could have been one shell at 4.00 in the morning; that would be consistent with the report, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, it must have been more than one shelling. Normally we do not pay very much attention to only one impact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told by BritBat how many shells were reported to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You simply reported what BritBat gave to you, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly in this case, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke of meeting then Colonel Blaskic at the Kiseljak barracks on, I believe, February 22nd 1993, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the first meeting I recall I had with him, a sort of introductory meeting, and of course as always when we met, we could not do without discussing the operational situation, that was what we were there for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Do you remember the dates or time periods of any other meetings you had with him in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just remember it must have been some date before the 16th April, because since then I think he more or less stuck to his headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read the transcript. I did not follow your testimony at that point. You are saying from mid April forward, he stuck to his headquarters in Vitez and stayed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, "stuck" is probably not the correct word to use, because I think he went out to his troops once in a while and had contact with them and not just by sitting behind his desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a war raging from 16th April on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what date or dates you met with him in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not until the last meeting that took place, last time was 9th May I recall, so-called farewell visit, and also again discussing operational stuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the dates of any other visits you had with him in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: on your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I had meetings, but not exactly the dates of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your trip to Kiseljak from -- strike that. On your trip to Kiseljak on 22nd February 1993, where did you originate from? What was the beginning point of your travels on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 22nd February?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, in other words where were you starting from on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the first meeting you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Were you in Kiseljak at the beginning of the day on 22nd February 1993, or did you -- please let me finish my question. We do not want to go too fast, so the interpreters have a fair chance to interpret. Were you there or did you have to travel there from some other location in order to get to your meeting with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I travelled from Busovaca along the road down to Kiseljak, had our meeting on the UN headquarters or made some buyings there from their stocks, and it was in the afternoon some time that we met Colonel Blaskic in his office there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in the course of those travels, did you have to pass -- by the way, did you travel on the Busovaca-Kiseljak road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to pass through various checkpoints of both the HVO and the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact the portion of the road from Bilalovac to Kacuni roughly was controlled by the BH army, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That had been the case since roughly 27th January 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic did not have free passage over that road, correct, at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seems to me he did not, but I also know that both parties are using their little tricky roads that they know around in the mountains which they can use for that purpose, or he can move the other way around from Zenica into Kiseljak by another route. You will see that on the map when you look on the terrain, there are other routes going into Kiseljak than just the one from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To go to Sarajevo you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To go to Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Visoko is one of the things, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Visoko was held by the BH army too, was it not, at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. But again I have to stress to you that the commanders from both sides knew their own tricky ways around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me this, Major: between 27th January 1993 and at least the second week in March 1993, can you tell us of any instance when Colonel Blaskic made it out of Kiseljak to Vitez other than in an UNPROFOR Warrior escorted for the purpose of an official UN meeting, any instance? Can you give us one instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because I think he would not tell us if he had other means of going around. That is correct, that UN, to certain meetings where he was required, transported him safely through all the checkpoints, the BiH checkpoints too, of course. That is correct, but that was the official means of coming to and from where we were involved. How he guided and controlled his own troops coming around, UN would not take care of that and we would not, ECMM, take care of bringing him around for his own people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You met with him in the HVO barracks in Kiseljak on 22nd February 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was in the brigade quarters, was he not, the Kiseljak brigade quarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we always met in the same room, I recall a special picture hanging on the wall and I think during the first meeting I asked Colonel Blaskic "who is that guy?", because he looked like a King, and I got some explanation about the old Croatian kings and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that Colonel Blaskic had a headquarters staff in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we heard it then or observed it that way that we met him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not ask, Major, whether you met him in Kiseljak, I understand you did. My question is a different one. He had a headquarters staff in Vitez, correct, at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information, any specific information suggesting that he had a headquarters staff in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day you went to Kiseljak and brought one or more civilians out with you, when was that? Was that a different occasion from your 22nd February visit, or the same occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was 18th April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where, if you know, where was Colonel Blaskic on 18th April? Was he in Kiseljak or was he in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not in Kiseljak. I suppose, I cannot tell for him where he was that day exactly, but I suppose he was in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can tell us, though, that he was not in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He might have been hiding, but he knew that EC monitors were there and I think he would like to talk to us if he knew that we came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because he always wanted to talk to you, did he not, if you were in his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we asked for having a meeting with him he was always willing to find a date where it could happen. It might not be the first time, it may be the second one and we were given the time where we could see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 18th April 1993 when you went to Kiseljak, did you pass through the same checkpoints and the same BiH Army-held strip of land, that is on the road from Busovaca to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the HVO commander you spoke with in Kiseljak on that occasion, 18th April; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall his name. He presented himself as a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that in the Busovaca joint commission meeting on 18th April, which I think you attended, there was an agreement between the HVO and the BH army to exchange lists of all prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This list was things that we, together with the Red Cross, on behalf of Red Cross, should provide, because Red Cross took care of prisoners. Whenever we came around and had a feeling or so or knew there were prisoners, we tried to collect as much information as we could get, try to free somebody if somebody was in need and if we were allowed to see the prisoners; if we were not always, then we handed over what we knew of information to International Red Cross, same day or a day after.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a meeting with a representative of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present at any meetings between the ICRC and Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not personally involved in that particular thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still have -- do you have still have Exhibit 187 with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means the 20th April report?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the ops report from 20th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look at page 2, paragraph 8C. This is a report, I take it, from Mr. Morsink, if I am pronouncing his name correctly, that he went with an ICRC rep to the HVO brigade headquarters at Vitez, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be the headquarters of Mario Cerkez at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO brigade headquarters was this Cerkez, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where the brigade was headquartered, not the command for the Operational Zone for Central Bosnia, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was shortly away in the next block of houses, or like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a different office, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a different office, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about your meeting with Ramiz Dugalic on 9th May 1993. Was it your testimony that he told you that in Ahmici two HVO soldiers were captured, or two HV soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They found in their pockets two HVO badges, that was what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it represented to you that they believed, that is Mr. Dugalic believed that there were HVO soldiers involved in the attack or HV soldiers. I may have misheard your testimony on direct, I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he believed it was HVO guys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you had a discussion about Darko Kraljevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well not a discussion, we were just told that a man behind, this Darko Kraljevic, he was a neighbour to somebody that we knew, who lived in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the usher could assist, I have two documents I would like provided to the witness as well as the court and counsel, an original in BSC and an English translation; I apologise there is no French translation at this point in time. My question for you, Major, is: at your meeting with Ramiz Dugalic, the deputy commander of III Corps BiH Army on 9th May 1993, he provided you with a document which you now have in your possession, namely the BSC copy of the document that you have been provided with, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall to have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to this meeting with another monitor, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, and he prepared a report that included --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, the witness was asked a very narrow line of questions about a conversation in respect of the truck bomb and Darko Kraljevic. We are now going into an area far broader than that and I would object, Mr. President, it is beyond the scope of the examination in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman, can you respond to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The statement of the other monitor who attended the same meeting as the witness states with respect to this document: "This is a licence that Muslims have to leave their homes, example at appendix 1." If you see at the top of the right-hand corner of the English translation, this document is an appendix to an ECMM report and this document was obtained by the ECMM in the very interview that the witness attended. Maybe he does not remember, but I think I have the right to try and refresh his recollection on that point. Perhaps it is even refreshed by the colloquy that we have had.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I be answering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I think that the question is not out of order, but I shall consult my colleagues. (Pause). Yes, Mr. Hayman. We are a bit on the boundary, but the Trial Chamber allows you to reformulate your question, but briefly, so please proceed, trying to focus more on what was covered by the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I only have a few more questions, Mr. President and your Honours. Thank you for the opportunity to refresh the witness's recollection on this point. Major, is your recollection refreshed by the colloquy you have heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is refreshed in that way, that in those days, although not any more, a chairman of any commission. I was put back in Zenica together with this McLeod who came from our superior headquarters in Zagreb. He was in charge, with my assistance, to try to collect all what we knew about atrocities, and reasons why and how many and so on were wounded, killed, and that is it, so therefore, as he was a man to make up the summary and made up his own report, which he did on 17th May, the same day I was leaving or the day before I was leaving, he got all the documents; that means also that he is more in the picture of keeping the details, because he had the document with him. I do not recall myself to have seen this document, I might have seen it just passing through me to McLeod. That is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he made it an appendix to the notes of your meeting with Ramiz Dugalic on that day, do you have any reason to doubt his report in that regard, that he obtained it at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not. We were working close and talking about what we saw and so on, and I was, as I told you, his assistant, who in some times made the notes for him, but in this case, I have only a few notes concerning that meeting, so I cannot say that I knew these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I offer the document, your Honour. It is taken from the ECMM report attached to the minutes of that meeting provided to the Defence by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object at this point in time. There is no proper foundation laid. The witness said he did not recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. The witness ended by saying that he cannot identify the document. Therefore I think this document should be placed in reserve. Judge Riad? It has not been identified, the document has not been formally identified by the witness, so we leave it aside for the moment and limit ourselves to what the witness said and which appears in the transcript. Next question, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: These two HVO soldiers that you were told by Commander Dugalic, did you meet with them, did you ever see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone from ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were told that Ante Valenta was a political advisor to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he introduced himself the first time to us, or the first time to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is how Valenta introduced himself to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in the presence of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure of that. No, I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not recall Colonel Blaskic being present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that, quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else ever tell you that other than Valenta himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my fellow monitors who know better than me in our Regional Centre in Zenica, told us about Ante Valenta, what position he held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and they were all told that his position was political advisor to Colonel Blaskic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told he had any other political position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the only position was that of advisor to Colonel Blaskic, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we knew it from the wartime we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described this threat from Mr. Valenta, or you believe it was him on the phone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 90 to 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not questioning you, believe me. In your meetings and conversations with Colonel Blaskic, did he ever threaten any harm towards ECMM, BritBat or any other international organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, he co-operated with ECMM, would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It seemed so, whenever we had a request, he tried to come forward to us and assist him. We experienced him as a so-called nice kind man with a soft glove over his iron fist, so to say. He seemed to be a strong commander but gently when that was needed and that was needed in case of us, if he wanted us to assist him, he tried to assist. It seemed so and it helped a number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this call from Mr. Valenta, was it before or after the truck bomb explosion in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after the car bomb, because he referred exactly to this big help that the Brits gave to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get my letter of April 24th 1997, requesting an interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1997? Yes, we got that. I remember, I got that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As I recall, you were personally willing to grant an interview, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object. Again, it is outside the scope of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I was sure you were going to object, Mr. Harmon, but I wanted you to express your entire objection. Is it one of principle, because Mr. Hayman has not finished his question. The Tribunal could know what the question is, but is it an objection of principle that you raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is an area I certainly could have gone into, I did not elect to go into. It is outside the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you will be able to answer in your re-examination, that is how the game is played, you know that Mr. Harmon, but before we say anything, I would like to know where Mr. Hayman is going. We want to see whether or not this is really going too far away from the examination-in-chief, so for the time being, Mr. Hayman, continue please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions in this area, Mr. President. You got my letter. On a personal level as I recall, you were willing to grant me an interview, is that right, in terms of your own personal feelings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were three Danish monitors who received that letter, I recall. We have a talk between us, we had a talk with our General, of the Danish army, if there was a correct legal procedure. According to Danish law, it is not quite correct, I would say it that way. There have been cases where this is indecent way, that the witness for the Prosecutor is now approached by the Defence to have talks with him and prepare things, and the end of that was, that was Lars Baggesen, one of my colleagues there, who answered your question, "you have our evidence", or you will be having our evidence about things, that is what you can see as the Prosecutor can see right now, so it is all in there and the rest is going to my opinion and to the General Advocate of Denmark's opinion too, that the rest is going to take place in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understood, did you not, as a result of those conversations, that the message sent to the Defence was, under Danish law, once a witness has spoken to the Prosecution, they are not allowed to speak to the other side, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No further questions. Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you want to re-examine, but I think that the last point -- do what you like, but this is a formal consideration. Mr. Harmon, if you have no specific points about that question, perhaps you have some other questions that you would like to ask in order to supplement your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me turn to the judges now, Judge Riad. Judge Riad has several questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major Friis-Pedersen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, honourable judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that in your general dealings with the HVO, and I quoted you, you considered General Blaskic as a strong commander.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You considered General Blaskic as a strong commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my feeling and the feeling of my co-monitors too, when we spoke about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was a decision maker or such people like Ante Valenta, or those who were around him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was, to my best opinion, the decision maker and the man in command and control of his area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was what they called, I am not sure I can point out the boundary today, but it was operational zone middle Bosnia, he was commander of those brigades within that area and that surely involved all of our area we are talking about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Major, do forgive me. I am referring to your summary report of 20th April 1993. It is in the admirable clipped language the military is accustomed to using.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know all those abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will bear with me for that reason, I seem unclear about something:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have in mind paragraph 3, the third line, and I refer to the words, "shelling HVO HQ and the PTT building in Vitez". Could you explain that in ordinary language for me, shelling by whom or from where and shelling what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, shelling the HVO HQ means headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shelling from there or shelling of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shelling on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shelling on the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shells were falling on the HVO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, someone fired somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: PTT means "post and telegraph".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that means shells were also raining down on the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to where these shells were coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was those two 34 tanks that were on the position of the mountain road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, now I have got --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, honourable judge, it was an unconfirmed information at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have got the picture you sought to project to your military colleagues, in language that must remain forever cryptic to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is sometimes the intention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it from what you have been telling us that you were particularly concerned about any contraventions of humanitarian principles, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was part of all monitors' job to look after -- not only the military situation, the municipality, local political organisation, all civilian stuff, all police stuff, because no really authority were working there, not for sure. Sometimes they worked, sometimes they even did their job properly, that they took care of both their own and the other part, sometimes not. So we had to take care of everything, but we worked together with International Red Cross, as mentioned, and we worked together with international -- the UNHCR, refugee organisation of the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you. So whenever there was need for you to speak to someone on the Croatian side about a possible contravention of humanitarian principles, who was the officer at the top with whom conversations would be held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we knew directly who to go to, who was in so-called local charge of the thing, we would approach him. If we foresaw any difficulty in that area, we would always go to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times, could you say how many times you personally met with Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been around, up to six times, something like that, during my period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here is an odd question, do your best to answer it if you can and if you cannot, then forego it. On the average, could you indicate to us what was the duration of each meeting, ten minutes, half an hour, one hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly around one hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in the course of these meetings, would you say you were able to acquire some personal acquaintance of General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand what I accomplished. Please say again, honourable judge. What should I accomplish? What was the question please again?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it differently. In the course of these six meetings, each of which would have endured for approximately one hour, would you say you came to know General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as good as you can do under those circumstances, as good that you can do during that serious talks, because it was a serious situation or serious situations we were facing, and then you sometimes get a little bit under the other one's skin. Yes, I would say that we knew him rather good, we thought, rather good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it it is against that background that you have described him as a strong commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. It is the appearance, of course. You cannot see what is behind the eyes or teeth or like that, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever say to you that there were military elements on the Croatian side who were operating beyond the reach of his command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was his claim on a number of times, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say on that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said if we claimed that HVO could have done this and that, that that was not his forces, it must have been uncontrolled elements from outside. I would add here to that, that was exactly the same thing we heard from the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were getting the same story from opposite quarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Blaskic indicate with any specificity what these outside forces might have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you with your interest in possible breaches of humanitarian principles ever speak with General Blaskic about his own responsibilities as the military commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that I have raised that issue with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Major, I have only one question. When we were talking about the meetings with the accused, you used the expression, at least in French you said that he was a -- he had an iron fist in a glove, that it was Talleyrand who used that expression in referring to Napoleon. I would like to ask you a question. He was not only polite and pleasant, but that he co-operated with you, and even said to you, I believe that Judge Riad checked on that, you said that every time you asked him for something, that he did everything he could in order to satisfy you. Could you give us some specific examples of requests in your area, which is the application of international humanitarian law and status of prisoners, international conventions; could you give us specific examples which would illustrate this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will try. We had a number of incidents where small convoys, humanitarian convoys were held, for hours, days, and the drivers taken away in prison, temporary. Humanitarian convoys who should go into BiH pockets or BiH enclaves. Where we brought this up with Colonel Blaskic, that is an example where we brought this up, and he promised to intervene, which happened in some cases, that we could free those guys to drive the convoy through to their termination point. I would not say that he was always co-operating, I would say that he was normally co-operating with us, so we felt that he was a man to go to, if anybody, that could maybe solve a specific situation. I hope that is answer enough, honourable judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Almost, not completely. I understand that you did cite an example, but I would like to have examples or an example for those subjects about which you felt strongly. You talked about humanitarian aid, but for other subjects that also were of importance to you, like the Geneva Conventions. Would you have one or several examples where he did not maintain his promises which would make you think that he was indifferent or it did not concern him, because you have just said, you yourself said, I am not telling you my own opinion, you said that you cited an example, but then you added that he was not always obliging. Could you explain what you mean? If not, then you will not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation as we had before 16th April, clearly it stressed that there were very much trouble about getting the route clear from Busovaca down to Kiseljak, where a number of checkpoints from both sides, our main task at that time would be, the monitors' main task would be to look after, that those checkpoints were abandoned, that the trenches were filled in, that the positions were withdrawn longer away so they cannot shoot at each other as they did nearly every day, and those things were brought also up with Colonel Blaskic. Even if he promised to do his part, putting pressure on his commanders, which we learned from his deputy commander, Mr. Nakic, who was with us every day in the joint commission, we did not succeed that, we nearly succeeded up until Easter, but we did not succeed all. The positions were still there, we had a little co-operation about mixing the checkpoints so there should be mixed HVO and BiH checkpoints where they were close to each other anyway, but Colonel Blaskic's orders, for one reason or another, we could not see the real impact of what he has ordered, even if he issued it in writing, said he has done so and so. I am not sure we got the full co-operation there, because he as a military commander should be and, as we understood it, was in power to enforce those things as the other party would also do, they promised the same thing. Is that sufficient, honourable judge?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I will have to be satisfied with that, because, of course, one might understand that a military commander in a situation like this cannot agree with all of your requests, especially when military matters are involved. I was more specifically thinking about the protection of refugees, protection of civilian persons or prisoners. However, unless you would like to add to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can add just a little thing, that Colonel Blaskic promised us to assist in any way he could concerning prisoners of war or prisoners, to have them free and co-operate with International Red Cross about it. I think that was one of those things that worked, it was working when I was leaving there anyway, that day after day they gave prisoners free from one prison, another prison, but that was mainly, those things were mainly run by International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a military chief, would you not say that he was doing what he could, given the situation? That is, in the situation that was there at the time? Can you think of any other reasons that he might have done what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew part of what was going on, military, from the one side and from the other side, so we could not look behind his back and see what he was doing when we have left any of those meetings or what he did concerning implementing what he has promised, but I would say that he was a commander that was exercising command and control; in which degree he really did it, that is up to his own morale and his own will at that spot at that time, but he should have and had the means of exercising command and control. But to my best opinion, as a military commander, having been that myself, it is sometimes difficult but, okay, war is a difficult thing, you can even die from it, which happens in a number of occasions in former Yugoslavia, we know that. He could also be in the danger zone. He could be squeezed between the zone, but it does not free him from the responsibility of exercising according to the rules you have to obey, nationally, internationally, as a military commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you for having tried to focus as best as possible you could for your answers. My colleague would like to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Major Friis-Pedersen, you have just mentioned that Colonel Blaskic mentioned sometimes to you that there are other forces interfering. Was this by any chance related to the events in Vitez or in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, among other things, but especially here when you point out Ahmici, it was there as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you develop with that more? Was there any specific thing which he denied being responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for claiming that he was not responsible for outside forces coming and doing something --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Outside forces, that was the impression that I heard several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be forces which are not HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be, that is just a guess, but I have to do that if you want to. It might be HV forces, which was however normally stationed or infiltrating down at the southern border of Bosnia-Herzegovina into Croatia. We have heard but not seen, or I have not seen personally, an HV marked soldier. They have another badge on and other marks. I have not either seen the black masks, that was a sort of terror group they have inside the HVO. That was what could have been referred to by Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But usually what you saw were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was what we saw always, or I saw always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. We have asked you many questions, and you have collaborated very well. I do not know if this is beyond what you were authorised to say by the Danish Government, but in any case, the Tribunal is very grateful for your testimony. We will now suspend this long part of our hearing and we will resume at 4.45, so we will take a 15 minute pause. (4.30 pm) (A short break) (4.45 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would call our next witness, but we need to do so in a closed session. The next witness is the witness we discussed previously in a session and will be testifying about information that is extremely sensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In line with the decision taken by the Chamber, you can call this witness and we will have a closed session. Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, I think it would be preferable to have a closed session, totally closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You agree, not partially, not a private session but a closed session? Very well, we are going to have a closed session. I have not forgotten, Mr. Hayman, that you have a motion to submit to us, and after this witness, you have another witness for tomorrow morning, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, perhaps we will start a little earlier tomorrow, we will see how it goes with this testimony, so I am pronouncing a closed session. I say so for the benefit of the public. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
