utterances.text: Very well. Then we will conclude this hearing, we will now go back into public hearing as requested by Mr. Hayman. We will hear what he has to say. Are we back in public session now? Yes, we are, so we can begin. The judges are listening to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and your Honours, for hearing the Defence. I will be brief. As the court knows, we submitted a motion on hearsay issues and while we think that it will be unusual for the court, perhaps unusual for the court to exclude hearsay statements, as we urged in our submission, we think there may be and will be some occasions where that would be the proper exercise of the court's discretion, and we feel compelled to raise that issue specifically with respect to the statements of Witness A attributed to the individual Cicko, in which it is related by Cicko that a certain state of mind existed or certain orders were given by the accused concerning the events in Ahmici. Why do we think that statement does not pass muster in terms of some minimum threshold of reliability? One, the Tribunal has been given no information concerning the basis of Cicko's knowledge for that information. Cicko may have been an officer in a diversionary group that fought against the Serbs in 1992. He was not an officer in the Jokers, he was a foot soldier in the Jokers. So any knowledge Cicko would have of any order that Colonel Blaskic did or did not give is many levels of hearsay removed from the purported speaker, perhaps four or five. Second, Witness A did not obtain the statement in a face-to-face encounter, it was overheard, and although Witness A stated that Witness A was confident of the identity of the speaker, that is Cicko, still it is qualitatively different from a statement made in a direct conversation between two individuals. That is number two. Number three, this court has not and to the Defence's knowledge will not receive any corroboration in this trial of any order issuing from Colonel Blaskic of the nature referenced by Witness A and attributed to Cicko, no corroboration. There certainly has been none to date. Four, Cicko has a motive to lie to the detriment of our client; one, our client sent Cicko, caused him to be imprisoned in February 1993 for the murder and blowing up of a Muslim and a Muslim home, and he remained in prison for some period as a result of our client's actions. In addition, it appears from the testimony before the court that Cicko resented and felt pressured by the investigation ordered by the accused into the events at Ahmici, and I am referring to Cicko's statements that he felt that he was being left to bear the brunt of responsibility for these atrocities. For those four reasons, we suggest that this hearsay quintuple, whatever it is, hearsay statement attributed to Cicko does not meet some basic reliability standard which we think the court should exercise in this situation. Lastly, we think the situation here is particularly serious because there is no showing that Cicko was unavailable; that is, there is no showing by the Prosecutor that Cicko was unavailable. In fact, they have confirmed he is not going to be a Prosecution witness and we have not been told that is because he is unavailable, we have been told, as far as I can tell, because they do not want to call him. What does that mean? That means they have the option of two sources of proof here. They have direct proof, the speaker, the declarant, and they have indirect derivative evidence through a very sympathetic witness who was presented to the court. Sympathetic does not do justice to that individual whom we heard from this morning. So they have chosen to present a messenger, a derivative witness when they had a direct witness, Cicko, who they could bring here, and by bringing in the derivative witness, they can shield the declarant speaker, the declarant, the speaker, Cicko, from any cross-examination by the Defence. We think that is very serious under all standards, including the European Commission on Human Rights. I am almost done, your Honours. I appreciate it is late. It is easy to say and to think, "these little bits of hearsay, they are not important, it is just a little bit here, a little bit there, why is the Defence so excited about this?". I think we have honestly seen in this case, we have seen more and more little bits presented through derivative, second, third hand witnesses. Just today, what have we heard from derivative witnesses where the primary witness could have appeared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand what you are saying, but I do not want to reargue the principle of hearsay. I do not want to go back to everything you have said up to this point, but I do not want us to go back to this discussion we have already had. We agree on that, do we not? What you have just said to us is exactly the introduction of your motion on the principle of hearsay. I would just like to recall that to you. Continue if you consider that you are not resuming arguments that have already been made.

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I just remind everyone we are in a public session. If Mr. Hayman is going to repeat in any detail testimony that was given in a closed session then it is not appropriate for us to remain in a public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I have avoided doing so to date, I do not intend to make any further statements about the testimony. If I have crossed a line, I apologise. I think I have been very scrupulous in that regard. Of course I do not mean to repeat myself. Let me just say I think this is serious because today, just today, we heard derivative evidence from Witness A in terms of Cicko's statement, we heard derivative evidence from Major Friis-Pedersen in terms of BritBat's report, source unreported, of shelling on Vitez on 20th April 1993 and now we have related through the last witness, and may I say in general terms the opinion of Cicko related by the last witness without identifying the last witness, I see no objection from the Prosecution, we have an opinion of Cicko, out of court declarant, that he thinks a document or set of documents is damaging to our client, again relayed by a messenger, we do not have the opportunity to confront Cicko. The Defence does not think these documents are damaging at all. Cicko's opinion to the contrary is something we should be allowed to confront. I am simply saying we believe this is an important issue, we submit it to the wise and sound discretion of your Honours, but I needed to put our specific thoughts regarding the Witness A comments on the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms. Paterson?

utterances.speaker: MS. PATERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was the Prosecutor that questioned Witness A. As you are aware, I am only a temporary participant in this trial, I have not been a participant since the beginning and I think it is better to defer to my colleague Mr. Kehoe to argue this, because I think he is more familiar with the history of this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I will be very brief concerning all of these issues raised by counsel. The issues that are raised by counsel are issues that simply go to the weight of any testimony that is brought before this Tribunal, plain and simple. The explanation as an apologist for the accused on behalf of Mr. Bralo notwithstanding the following remains true, that concerning this conversation that we heard this morning, Cicko was clearly involved in the operations and the massacre in Ahmici. He was a member of the HVO, as these documents attest, not only signed by the accused but also the orders that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Remember we are in a public session, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am just talking about the particular documents. The circumstances, Mr. President, under which the conversations regarding Bralo were made gave it a strong indicia of reliability. Bralo was sitting there talking to his friends about the aftermath of Ahmici, and about how everybody is running for cover. It has a strong indicia of reliability and the witness, of course, knew this man's voice. For the Defence counsel to argue that Bralo had some axe to grind because the accused had Bralo arrested simply flies in the face of reality. The reality of the situation is that Bralo walked in and out of that jail any time he pleased. If he wanted to go down to the pub and have a beer, that is what he did. If he wanted to go home for the weekend to see his wife, he did that too. When it came down to the time of the fighting, your Honours, on 16th April, he was released. I give you the pattern of conduct leading up to this because for all practical terms, Bralo came and went as he pleased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Going to the final argument, the final argument of counsel concerning the ability of the Prosecutor to go down to that area and bring this particular declarant, Miroslav Bralo, to the court, I think is -- I do not know quite how to describe it. The reality of the situation is we can not even get compliance with a court ordered subpoena of the government. I think it is completely unrealistic to expect that this individual is going to comply with any type of order of this court and come here to testify. The bottom line for all of this, your Honours, is the concerns being raised are concerns that go to the weight of this evidence. There will be additional evidence brought to this Chamber's attention to support what I have just declared on the record. At the end of the day, your Honours, the court I am sure will weigh all of that evidence in coming to the conclusion to see what weight it will give to one piece of evidence as opposed to the next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, you wish to reply? You do not have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: In less than a minute, your Honours. Assuming the individual will not come voluntarily, I think the court has the power to issue a material witness warrant, a warrant for the arrest of someone who has material information to the case, and to bring him here, particularly if it is easy to exercise that warrant. With respect to Bralo's incarceration, he was incarcerated, he was incarcerated on the orders of our client, he was not released on the orders or with the acquiescence of our client prior to 16th April and I do not think the Prosecutor is proffering that he was. Clearly he was out by 16th April and he participated in the Ahmici atrocities. That was not on the order or with the acquiescence of our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Pause). Mr. Hayman, first of all the Tribunal wants to acknowledge your motion and understands that this is a question which is very important for you in your Defence of General Blaskic. Judges have noted the arguments of both the parties and the greater or lesser degree of fragility of this evidence, but let the Tribunal come to its own conclusions as to the reliability of the evidence. At the time when you present your case, you will be able to propose any measures which seem useful for you in order to make that testimony even more fragile before the judges. It is exactly 6.00 now -- Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will be brief. We would request that the last four exhibits that were admitted in closed session be admitted under seal. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: With the reservations expressed by Mr. Hayman. Do you wish to intervene, yet again, Mr. Hayman? Tomorrow's hearing, since we have only one witness, but it might still begin at 9.30. The hearing is adjourned. (6.00 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 9.30 am the following day)
